metadata.title: TMUA 2020 · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and up to three matching follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both problems simplify a radical quotient into a sum of fractional powers and then apply the power rule.
Both differentiate a polynomial numerator divided by a fractional power; this version adds one preliminary square expansion.
The same radical-quotient simplification and differentiation are followed by evaluating the derivative at a specified input.
sharedKnowledge: distinguish function value from derivative value

matches.rationale: A supplied linear factor determines an unknown polynomial coefficient through substitution, then the remaining factors are recovered.
A linear factor again becomes a zero-substitution condition on a parameter; the resulting parameter equation is quadratic.
The same evaluate-at-the-divisor-zero mechanism is used with a nonzero remainder, extending the factor-theorem case.
This isolates the original’s cubic product sign-chart step, including all three zero boundaries and strict endpoints.

Both determine strict polynomial sign sets and intersect the component restrictions. The 2017 task additionally constructs a single quadratic inequality representing that overlap; the 2020 task asks for the interval directly.
The factors are trigonometric, but the deciding mechanism is still a product sign chart on ordered boundaries, not solving the factors independently.
sharedKnowledge: Find all factor zeros in the domain
combine signs at the same input

matches.rationale: Nonconsecutive GP terms are required to be consecutive AP terms; eliminate the AP difference, restrict the ratio and use an infinite sum.
The same numbers occur in different AP/GP orders, requiring careful position equations and elimination before a sum can be found.
AP and GP term equations eliminate the AP difference and give two possible ratios, of which convergence selects one.
Both recover quadratic coefficients from a specified vertex or axis plus one further graph condition.
Both use a single intersection as a repeated-root constraint to determine quadratic parameters.
This transfers the quadratic-symmetry step: the roots are symmetric about the axis, and an additional root-gap condition fixes the remaining coefficient.
sharedKnowledge: Root midpoint is the symmetry axis

matches.rationale: Both replace a repeated exponential by a positive variable and complete a quadratic square, checking the extremal input is attainable.
After a polynomial derivative step, the same reciprocal optimisation appears: minimise an everywhere-positive quadratic denominator.
Both optimise a quadratic after exponential substitution; this version additionally requires carrying a bounded sine-generated range.
Both simplify simultaneous exponential equations before solving algebraically, then use a same-base exponent relation for the requested combination.

Both rewrite powers to a common base and equate their exponents. The candidate then introduces a positive exponential variable and solves a quadratic; the original instead obtains simultaneous linear exponent equations.
This transfers the same index-law step by combining exponential factors first, then extracting the unknown exponent with logarithms.
Both convert a condition for every real x into a strict parameter inequality by controlling a quadratic’s extremum.
Both first find a quadratic’s vertex height as a function of its parameter and then analyse that second quadratic.
This transfers the second optimisation stage: find the requested quantity as a parameter quadratic, then complete its square.
Both build a new polynomial from transformed roots using their sum and product, without solving the original quadratic individually.
Both use the identity (a+b)²=a²+b²+2ab to recover missing symmetric root information and construct a quadratic.
sharedKnowledge: cross term in a squared sum

matches.rationale: This targets the original’s square-root sign step and its explicit-surds alternative: recognise squared surd forms and retain only principal nonnegative roots.
sharedKnowledge: choose the positive branch before adding

matches.rationale: Both apply a reflection and horizontal translation to a graph formula, preserving operation order and the inverse input shift.
sharedKnowledge: horizontal shifts act inside the function

matches.rationale: This isolates the horizontal scaling and translation mechanisms, checking them through the motion of a quadratic vertex.
sharedKnowledge: Equate new inner input with old input

matches.rationale: The same ordered translation-reflection-scaling reasoning is transferred to a circle, tracking a reference point and length scale separately.
Both convert separately positive lobe areas into signed integral equations. The follow-up requires reconstructing three unsigned areas from overlapping signed totals.
Both use the difference between positive and negative contributions to recover area information. The follow-up also applies a reflection after finding the separate area magnitudes.
Both count intersections between a periodic trigonometric curve and a nonperiodic curve, using domain, signs and individual branches instead of exact root formulas.
Both restrict the allowed trigonometric branches and count their intersections with a simple monotone curve. The follow-up adds safe division and an angle multiplier.
Both use the range of a trigonometric expression to restrict a nonperiodic curve, then count intersections on a combined sketch. The follow-up includes a central touching point.
Both extract a coefficient by identifying how powers can be selected from repeated factors. The follow-up has two distinct degree patterns and numerical multipliers.
Both require all combinations of factor terms producing one target power. This transfer uses convolution between two expansions rather than selecting two variables in one multinomial.
Both avoid full expansion by tracking only choices capable of producing the required power. The follow-up adds cancellation of constants before an outer multiplication.
Both need unsigned total area across regions of opposite sign and use symmetry to reduce integration. The follow-up makes the axis crossings fixed rather than parameter-dependent.
Both find parameter-dependent intersections, identify the upper curve and integrate the vertical gap. The follow-up checks a square-root domain before using a power antiderivative.
Both use symmetry to compute one half of an enclosed region and double its positive area. The follow-up requires choosing the correct absolute-value branch first.
Both replace logarithmic expressions with algebraic variables, solve a quadratic, then exponentiate back before calculating the requested quantity.
Both combine logarithm laws with a quadratic reduction and require checking the original logarithm domains. The follow-up transfers this to simultaneous equations.
Both turn an exponential or logarithmic equation into a quadratic in a hidden variable, filter its domain and calculate a difference only after returning to the original variable.
Both read a circle’s centre and radius, use the perpendicular tangent radius and form a right triangle to recover a slope-related quantity.
The original distinguishes the geometry of common tangents; this transfer reinforces centre-distance and radius relations and the difference between internal and external contact.

This transfer isolates the prerequisite centre-and-radius geometry used in the original: extract centres, calculate their distance with Pythagoras and retain exact surds. It does not repeat the tangent-angle step.

Both count intersections only in a restricted domain and identify parameter values where two intersections merge or one becomes inadmissible. The ray plays the role of the nonnegative square-root variable.

Both use a quadratic substitution with a restricted real range and combine discriminant, root sum and root product to count the original real solutions. The original allows zero transformed roots and has an acknowledged missing c=0 option; the candidate requires strictly positive roots for four distinct quartic roots.
sharedKnowledge: Both use a quadratic substitution with a restricted real range and combine discriminant, root sum and root product to count the original real solutions. The original allows zero transformed roots and has an acknowledged missing c=0 option; the candidate requires strictly positive roots for four distinct quartic roots.

matches.rationale: This follow-up isolates the discriminant and degree conditions used in the original. Its explicit nonzero parameter also highlights why leading-coefficient and boundary cases must be checked.
Both reduce a trigonometric equation to a quadratic in a nonnegative expression, reject an out-of-range root, then recover every permitted cosine sign.

Both preserve sign cases when a trigonometric magnitude is represented by an absolute value and check the full stated angular domain. The candidate introduces its modulus through principal square roots and counts sign-cancellation quadrants; the original already has a modulus and solves a quadratic for exact cosine levels.
Both use two square-root sign branches and then count trigonometric solutions on the specified interval. The follow-up also scales the angle interval by three.
Both seek the least positive integer satisfying a strict quadratic inequality. The follow-up first derives that inequality from an integral and sum, then checks the first integer above the boundary.

Both convert a strict algebraic threshold into a permitted set of integers and check the original restrictions. This transfer adds a convergence domain and counts the surviving integers for a probability.
Both count distinct roots of a parameter-dependent product and locate parameter values where roots coincide. Each requires a separate zero-parameter case and careful union of root sets.
Both count a union of factor zero sets without double-counting a common root. The follow-up transfers this to xf′(x) and constructs examples to realise different counts.
sharedKnowledge: Both count a union of factor zero sets without double-counting a common root. The follow-up transfers this to xf′(x) and constructs examples to realise different counts.

matches.rationale: Both classify real-root counts as a parameter changes and explicitly check the repeated-root boundary. The follow-up adds the logical distinction between a full range and a sufficient condition.
